newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-SPAIN OFFERS LATIN AMERICANS SHORT CUT TO CITIZENSHIP.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SPAIN OFFERS LATIN AMERICANS SHORT CUT TO CITIZENSHIP.

text.p: Latin American players are rushing to take out Spanish citizenship in a back door entry to lucrative European soccer careers opened up by the Bosman ruling.
So far more than 20 Latin Americans have taken out Spanish nationality, taking advantage of a law which makes them eligible for citizenship after just two years' residence.

The legal manoeuvre allows them to move freely in European Union countries, benefiting both themselves and their Spanish hosts as it provides the national team with an unexpected new source of potential players.

Last year's Bosman ruling outlawed quotas on European Union (EU) players but left intact limits on the number of other foreigners who are allowed to play in national leagues within the European community.

Last week Chilean striker Ivan Zamorano -- who met residency qualifications while playing for Sevilla and Real Madrid -- took up Spanish nationality too so that he would no longer be considered a foreigner at his new club, Italy's Inter Milan.
Zamorano's change of status not only freed Inter to use an additional non-EU player in their line-up but also increased the player's value in the transfer market.
Some reports have suggested the club made Zamorano's adoption of dual nationality a condition for signing him.
Many more South Americans are set to follow suit and several have already made the move, among them Real Madrid midfielder Fernando Redondo from Argentina.
"I'm very happy. I feel Spanish and, with the Bosman law, it is an advantage," said Redondo after swearing to observe the Spanish constitution earlier this season.
Fellow-Argentine internationals Diego Simeone and Juan Eduardo Esnaider, who play for neighbours Atletico, are also expected to be given Spanish passports in the near future.
In addition to being Spanish, all three will keep their existing nationalities and be eligible for Argentina.
But players who have not been capped for their native countries will be available to play for Spain at international level.
Rayo Vallecano's Brazilian Guilherme is tipped as a future front-man for Javier Clemente's Spanish side after the end of December, the second anniversary of his arrival in the country.

Tenerife goalkeeper Marcelo Ojeda should have his papers within a matter of weeks and could join Barcelona forward Juan Pizzi as a successor in the Spanish line-up to another Hispano-Argentine, legendary striker Alfredo di Stefano.
Pizzi has won 14 caps since getting his papers while at Tenerife, a destination favoured by many Latin Americans.

For Brazilians the favourite club is undoubtedly Deportivo Coruna, where the local language is similar to their native Portuguese. Midfielder Donato has already turned out for Spain on several occasions, while Deportivo team mate Mauro Silva has become Spanish but continues to play for Brazil.
Espanyol striker Miguel Angel Benitez is now Spanish-Paraguayan and team mate Mauricio Pochettino is likely to become Spanish-Argentine within the next few weeks.
A dozen or more players from the first and second division are expected to begin the process soon.
In the past, several players have even falsified documents to push through naturalisation. In one case the chicanery of an Argentine basketball player cost his side promotion.

While the Bosman law has given a clear advantage to EU players, the Spanish football authorities' decision to increase the number of other foreigners allowed by teams from three to four has also opened up new avenues.
The Spanish league is now awash with Russians, players from the former Yugoslav republics and especially Brazilians.

Once thought a risky bet by many Spanish clubs, the Brazilians have arrived in force to fill the spaces left by the 29 EU players in the first division who are no longer considered foreigners because of the Bosman case.
